## 1. Introduction and installation

### What does Routbreak calculate?

Routbreak describes early epidemic emergence when population groups are
connected. Given a reproduction matrix, it calculates:

- the probability that an introduction produces a non-extinct transmission
  chain;
- the introduction-specific outbreak reproduction ratio, `R_ob`;
- local and total reproduction for each group; and
- the system-level reference reproduction ratio, `R_ref`.

Throughout Routbreak, **rows are infection destinations and columns are
infection sources**. Thus `R[i, j]` is the expected number of infections in
destination group `i` produced by one infected individual from source group
`j`.

Routbreak is not yet available from CRAN. Install it from GitHub with:

```{r install-routbreak, eval=FALSE}
install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github("peasantxuan/Routbreak")
```

The survey-data example later in this tutorial uses `socialmixr`, a suggested
package available from CRAN. Its bundled POLYMOD survey lets the example run
offline; Routbreak does not download or redistribute those records.

## 2. A minimal reproduction matrix

### How is a connected population represented?

Consider three hypothetical communities. The names on both dimensions make
the matrix convention explicit.

```{r minimal-matrix}
library(Routbreak)

community <- c("North", "Central", "Coast")

R <- matrix(
  c(
    0.95, 0.12, 0.05,
    0.35, 0.85, 0.12,
    0.12, 0.25, 1.05
  ),
  nrow = 3,
  byrow = TRUE,
  dimnames = list(destination = community, source = community)
)
R
```

Column `"North"` contains infections generated by a source case in North.
Row `"North"` contains infections arriving in North from all three sources.
For example, `R["Central", "North"]` is the expected number of Central
infections generated by one North source case.

```{r orientation-check, results='hide'}
R[, "North"]
R["North", ]

stopifnot(
  identical(rownames(R), colnames(R)),
  all(is.finite(R)),
  all(R >= 0)
)
```

## 3. Basic Routbreak metrics

### What does one introduction imply for each community?

`rob_table()` calculates the main quantities together, reusing the outbreak
probabilities internally.

```{r basic-results}
risk <- rob_table(R)
risk
```

Each row corresponds to the source community where infection is introduced:

- `outbreak_probability` is the probability that the early branching process
  does not eventually become extinct. It is not the final epidemic size.
- `R_ob` contrasts offspring production conditional on emergence with
  offspring production conditional on extinction.
- `R_local` is the diagonal entry of `R`, counting infections that remain in
  the source community.
- `R_total` is the source-column sum, counting infections generated across all
  destinations.
- `R_ref` is the spectral radius of the complete connected system. It is
  repeated in each row only to simplify comparison.

The same quantities are available separately through `outbreak_prob()`,
`r_ob()`, `r_local()`, `r_total()`, and `r_ref()` when only one output is
needed.

The introduction locations share one system-level `R_ref`, but their outbreak
probabilities and `R_ob` values differ because they enter different parts of
the connected transmission system. `R_local` alone misses exported
transmission, while `R_total` does not account for the future paths reached by
those exported infections.

## 4. Compare the reproduction metrics

### How does outbreak probability vary by introduction community?

```{r basic-probability-plot, fig.width=5.2, fig.height=3.1, out.width="70%", fig.align="center", fig.pos="H", fig.cap="Outbreak probability for an introduction into each community in the hypothetical three-community system."}
local({
  old_par <- par(no.readonly = TRUE)
  on.exit(par(old_par), add = TRUE)
  par(mar = c(4.2, 4.2, 1.2, 0.8))
  x <- seq_len(nrow(risk))
  plot(
    x, risk$outbreak_probability,
    type = "o", pch = 16, lwd = 2, col = "#0072B2", xaxt = "n",
    ylim = c(0, 1), xlab = "Introduction community",
    ylab = "Outbreak probability"
  )
  axis(1, at = x, labels = risk$community)
  text(
    x, risk$outbreak_probability,
    labels = sprintf("%.3f", risk$outbreak_probability),
    pos = 3, cex = 0.82, col = "#0072B2"
  )
})
```

The probability of epidemic emergence is highest for an introduction in
North and lower for introductions in Central or Coast. These probabilities
differ even though all three communities belong to the same connected system
and therefore share one `R_ref`.

### How do the reproduction ratios differ?

The following plot compares the introduction-specific and local quantities
with the common system-level reference value.

```{r basic-comparison-plot, fig.width=5.4, fig.height=3.1, out.width="75%", fig.align="center", fig.pos="H", fig.cap="Outbreak, local, and reference reproduction ratios for the hypothetical three-community system."}
local({
  old_par <- par(no.readonly = TRUE)
  on.exit(par(old_par), add = TRUE)

  par(mar = c(4.2, 4.2, 3.2, 0.8))
  x <- seq_along(community)
  matplot(
    x, cbind(risk$R_ob, risk$R_local), type = "o",
    pch = c(16, 17), lty = c(1, 2), lwd = 2,
    col = c("#0072B2", "#D55E00"), xaxt = "n",
    ylim = range(risk[, c("R_ob", "R_local", "R_ref")]),
    xlab = "Introduction community", ylab = "Reproduction ratio"
  )
  abline(h = unique(risk$R_ref), lwd = 2, lty = 3, col = "#009E73")
  axis(1, at = x, labels = risk$community)
  legend(
    "top", inset = c(0, -0.28), xpd = NA, horiz = TRUE,
    legend = c(expression(R[ob]), expression(R[local]), expression(R[ref])),
    col = c("#0072B2", "#D55E00", "#009E73"), lty = c(1, 2, 3),
    pch = c(16, 17, NA), lwd = 2, bty = "n"
  )
})
```

Overdispersed offspring and reproduction-matrix inference are covered in the
[negative-binomial](negative-binomial.html) and
[estimation](estimating-rob.html) tutorials.

## 5. Survey-data example: age-structured contacts in Italy

### How is the Italian contact matrix constructed?

The POLYMOD study recorded one day of contacts for participants in eight
European countries during 2005--2006. The `socialmixr` CRAN package includes
version 1.1 of these survey records. Its Italian subset has 849 participant
records. With the explicit missing-age handling below, 842 participants
contribute to the contact matrix. Participant and contact ages are grouped
into 5-year bands from 0--4 through 75--79, plus an 80+ group.

`socialmixr::contact_matrix()` returns the mean number of contacts reported by
each participant age group in **rows**, with contacted age groups in
**columns**. Thus its matrix has source rows and destination columns. The call
below uses the observed Italian survey participants within each age band. It
does not apply an external national population distribution, age weights, or
a reciprocity adjustment; the 17 analytic group counts range from 5 to 93
participants.

```{r socialmixr-availability, echo=FALSE}
if (!has_socialmixr) {
  message("The optional Italian POLYMOD example is skipped because socialmixr is not installed.")
}
```

```{r polymod-italy, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, eval=has_socialmixr}
data("polymod", package = "socialmixr")

italy_contacts <- socialmixr::contact_matrix(
  survey = polymod,
  countries = "Italy",
  age_limits = seq(0, 80, by = 5),
  symmetric = FALSE,
  estimated_participant_age = "mean",
  estimated_contact_age = "mean",
  missing_participant_age = "remove",
  missing_contact_age = "remove"
)

C_italy <- italy_contacts$matrix
age_group <- c(paste(seq(0, 75, 5), seq(4, 79, 5), sep = "-"), "80+")
dimnames(C_italy) <- list(source = age_group, destination = age_group)

survey_basis <- italy_contacts$participants
available_Italian_participants <- sum(
  as.character(polymod$participants$country) == "Italy"
)
data.frame(
  available_Italian_participants,
  participants_in_contact_matrix = sum(survey_basis$participants),
  minimum_per_age_group = min(survey_basis$participants),
  maximum_per_age_group = max(survey_basis$participants)
)
```

### How is the contact matrix converted to a reproduction matrix?

For this teaching scenario, every reported contact is assigned the same
expected transmission multiplier $\beta$. Susceptibility, infectiousness, and
infectious-period scaling are therefore uniform across age groups. If
$C_{sj}$ is the mean number of contacts that a participant in source group
$s$ reports with destination group $j$, then

$$
R_{js}=\beta C_{sj}.
$$

The transpose below is required only to convert the documented `socialmixr`
orientation to Routbreak's destination-row/source-column convention. Scaling
sets the illustrative system-level value to `R_ref = 1.5`; this value is not
an empirical estimate for Italy.

```{r polymod-reproduction-matrix, eval=has_socialmixr}
A_italy <- t(C_italy)
dimnames(A_italy) <- list(destination = age_group, source = age_group)
R_italy <- scale_to_rref(A_italy, target = 1.5)

result_italy <- rob_table(R_italy)
print(result_italy, digits = 4)
```

Each entry of `R_italy` is the expected number of infections in a destination
age group generated by an infected source age group under this uniform
per-contact scenario. Routbreak calculates outbreak probability, `R_ob`,
`R_local`, `R_total`, and the common `R_ref` for each introduction group.

### Does the generated matrix pass the required checks?

```{r polymod-validation, eval=has_socialmixr}
diagnostics_italy <- matrix_diagnostics(R_italy)

r_ref(R_italy)
is_irreducible(R_italy)
unique(diagnostics_italy[c(
  "component_size", "cyclic_period", "primitive_component",
  "matrix_irreducible"
)])

italy_metrics <- c("outbreak_probability", "R_ob", "R_local", "R_total")
italy_summary <- t(vapply(
  result_italy[italy_metrics],
  function(x) c(minimum = min(x), maximum = max(x), sd = sd(x)),
  numeric(3)
))
italy_summary

italy_spearman <- cor(
  result_italy[italy_metrics],
  method = "spearman"
)
round(italy_spearman, 3)
```

```{r polymod-assertions, include=FALSE, eval=has_socialmixr}
stopifnot(
  identical(available_Italian_participants, 849L),
  identical(sum(survey_basis$participants), 842L),
  identical(dim(C_italy), c(17L, 17L)),
  identical(dim(R_italy), c(17L, 17L)),
  identical(rownames(R_italy), colnames(R_italy)),
  all(is.finite(R_italy)),
  all(R_italy >= 0),
  abs(r_ref(R_italy) - 1.5) < 1e-12,
  all(diagnostics_italy$matrix_irreducible),
  all(diagnostics_italy$primitive_component)
)
```

The generated matrix is irreducible and primitive, with spectral radius 1.5.
`r_ref()` confirms the requested system-level normalization;
`is_irreducible()` confirms that every age group can reach every other through
positive transmission paths. `matrix_diagnostics()` additionally reports one
strongly connected component with cyclic period 1, so the matrix is primitive.
It produces genuine age-type variation: outbreak probability ranges from
0.203 to 0.701, `R_ob` from 1.118 to 1.723, `R_local` from 0.014 to 1.215,
and `R_total` from 0.568 to 1.977. These rounded values are calculated by the
preceding code when the optional package is available.

For these 17 groups, Spearman's rank correlation is 0.985 between outbreak
probability and `R_total`, and 0.777 between outbreak probability and
`R_local`. Outbreak probability and Poisson
`R_ob` have rank correlation 1 because `R_ob = -log(1-p)/p` is strictly
increasing for positive $p$. `R_ref` is constant and therefore has no defined
rank correlation with the age-specific metrics.

### How does outbreak probability vary by introduction age group?

```{r polymod-probability-plot, fig.width=7.4, fig.height=3.6, fig.pos="H", eval=has_socialmixr, fig.cap="Illustrative outbreak probability by introduction age group after scaling the Italian POLYMOD contact matrix to a reference reproduction ratio of 1.5."}
local({
  old_par <- par(no.readonly = TRUE)
  on.exit(par(old_par), add = TRUE)
  par(mar = c(4.8, 4.2, 1.2, 0.8))
  x_age <- seq_len(nrow(result_italy))
  plot(
    x_age, result_italy$outbreak_probability,
    type = "o", pch = 16, lwd = 2, col = "#0072B2", xaxt = "n",
    ylim = c(0, 1), xlab = "Source age group at introduction",
    ylab = "Outbreak probability"
  )
  axis(
    1, at = x_age, labels = result_italy$community,
    las = 2, cex.axis = 0.72
  )
})
```

The reproduction matrix has one common system-level `R_ref` of 1.5, but its
survey-derived age-contact
structure gives different introduction age groups different probabilities of
epidemic emergence. These are illustrative model outputs under uniform
per-contact transmission, not measured age-specific risks for a particular
epidemic.

### How do the age-specific reproduction ratios compare?

```{r polymod-reproduction-plot, fig.width=7.4, fig.height=3.7, fig.pos="H", eval=has_socialmixr, fig.cap="Age-specific outbreak and local reproduction ratios for the illustrative Italian POLYMOD scenario. The horizontal line is the chosen system-level reference reproduction ratio of 1.5."}
local({
  old_par <- par(no.readonly = TRUE)
  on.exit(par(old_par), add = TRUE)

  par(mar = c(4.8, 4.2, 3.2, 0.8))
  x_age <- seq_len(nrow(result_italy))
  matplot(
    x_age, result_italy[c("R_ob", "R_local")], type = "o",
    pch = c(16, 17), lty = c(1, 2), lwd = 2,
    col = c("#0072B2", "#D55E00"), xaxt = "n",
    ylim = range(result_italy[c("R_ob", "R_local", "R_ref")]),
    xlab = "Source age group at introduction", ylab = "Reproduction ratio"
  )
  abline(h = unique(result_italy$R_ref), lwd = 2, lty = 3, col = "#009E73")
  axis(1, at = x_age, labels = result_italy$community, las = 2, cex.axis = 0.72)
  legend(
    "top", inset = c(0, -0.25), xpd = NA, horiz = TRUE,
    legend = c(expression(R[ob]), expression(R[local]), expression(R[ref])),
    col = c("#0072B2", "#D55E00", "#009E73"),
    lty = c(1, 2, 3), pch = c(16, 17, NA), lwd = 2, bty = "n"
  )
})
```

`R_local` counts infections that remain within the source age group. `R_ob`
uses the entire age-connected system and conditions on whether transmission
survives. The common `R_ref` remains a property of the full 17-group matrix.

**Assumptions.** This example uses an unsymmetrized mean contact matrix from
the Italian POLYMOD survey sample and a Poisson multitype branching process.
It assumes a common transmission contribution per reported contact and uniform
susceptibility, infectiousness, and duration scaling. It does not adjust the
survey to a national age distribution. The calculations describe early
non-extinction under this illustrative model; they do not estimate final
epidemic size or establish empirical age-specific risks for a pathogen or time
period.

### Reproducibility

Package versions used to generate this example:

```{r polymod-versions, echo=FALSE, eval=has_socialmixr}
data.frame(
  package = c("Routbreak", "socialmixr"),
  version = c(
    as.character(packageVersion("Routbreak")),
    as.character(packageVersion("socialmixr"))
  )
)
```

## 6. Use your own matrix

### What information must a matrix provide?

Supply a finite, nonnegative square matrix with the same unique community
identifiers on its destination rows and source columns. Record the time scale,
population definitions, and scientific process used to construct every entry.

```{r own-matrix}
my_R <- matrix(
  c(1.1, 0.2, 0.1, 0.9),
  nrow = 2,
  byrow = TRUE,
  dimnames = list(
    destination = c("Group A", "Group B"),
    source = c("Group A", "Group B")
  )
)

rob_table(my_R)
```

For long-format data, `as_rmatrix()` requires explicit column names and does
not interpret missing edges as zero unless requested.

```{r long-format}
edges <- data.frame(
  source = c("A", "A", "B", "B"),
  destination = c("A", "B", "A", "B"),
  expected_infections = c(1.1, 0.1, 0.2, 0.9)
)

as_rmatrix(
  edges,
  source = "source",
  destination = "destination",
  value = "expected_infections"
)
```

Generation-resolved transmission data require a different workflow. See
[Estimating outbreak reproduction ratios from early transmission data](estimating-rob.html)
for explicit priors, previous-generation exposure indexing, and posterior
credible intervals.
